description.summary: A malevolent fairy king from Germanic and Scandinavian folklore who lures children to their death. The Erlking appears only to those doomed to die and is most famous from Goethe's 1782 poem.
description.full: The Erlking (Erlkönig) is a malevolent supernatural being from Germanic and Scandinavian folklore, representing a powerful and deadly fairy king. The name derives from a mistranslation of the Danish 'Ellerkonge' (alder king or elf king) into German. In folklore and literature, the Erlking appears specifically to children, invisible to adults, and lures them to death with promises of gifts and games. The most famous depiction comes from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's 1782 ballad 'Erlkönig,' later set to music by Franz Schubert, which tells of a child who sees the Erlking while riding through the night with his father and dies in his father's arms. The figure symbolizes death personified, childhood vulnerability to illness, and parental helplessness in the face of mortality.

etymology.origin: Mistranslation of Danish 'Ellerkonge' (alder king/elf king) to German 'Erlkönig' (Elf King) by Johann Gottfried Herder
etymology.meaning: Elf King - though originally may have meant Alder King, a nature spirit associated with alder trees

features.description: Varies from beautiful to terrifying; sometimes appears as handsome king, other times as skeletal or monstrous figure
Wears a crown denoting fairy royalty
Often depicted in flowing robes or regal garments
Sometimes accompanied by beautiful daughters who entice children

physical.morphology: Supernatural fairy being, appearance shifts between alluring beauty and terrifying death figure

abilities.description: Only children and the doomed can see the Erlking
Calls to children with promises of gifts, games, and treasures
Taking a child who follows means certain death
Can appear beautiful or terrifying depending on interpretation

patterns: Calls to children in gentle, seductive voice
Takes children who respond to his call

range.description: Germanic and Scandinavian folklore tradition, spread through literature across Europe

distribution.cultural_context: Germanic and Scandinavian cultural tradition, part of broader European fae folklore

literary_peak.description: Romantic era literary treatment, especially Goethe's poem and Schubert's lied

origins.cultural_roots: Germanic and Scandinavian folklore involving malevolent nature spirits and fairy kings who steal children
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to broader European traditions of child-stealing fairies, wild hunt, and death omens

timeline.significance: Erlking/Ellerkonge exists in Germanic and Scandinavian oral traditions
Johann Gottfried Herder translates Danish ballad, creating 'Erlkönig' name
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe writes famous ballad that defines modern conception
Franz Schubert composes art song setting of Goethe's poem, ensuring lasting cultural impact
Erlking becomes iconic figure in Romantic literature and music across Europe

history.modern_era: The Erlking remains primarily an artistic and literary figure, referenced in fantasy literature, music, and as cultural symbol of childhood vulnerability and death. Influences modern fantasy depictions of malevolent fae.

musical_settings.title: Erlkönig

interpretations: Parental helplessness in face of child's death
themes: The supernatural invisible to rational adults
